edges.description: Loss of amplification appears first in the basal, high-frequency cochlea. The intermediates between an under-damped amplifier in a young null mouse and a measurable human high-frequency threshold shift are not established, which is why the link is recorded as indirect: the mouse data show instability decades before threshold loss and then threshold loss with an intact hair cell complement, but nothing traces the intervening steps.
Progression follows the age-accelerated degradation of the tectorial membrane rather than hair cell loss, which is what the twelve-month null timepoint shows.
Reproduces the structural endpoint - reduced beta-tectorin, no striated-sheet matrix, absent Hensen's stripe - at the scale the node describes.
edges.limitations: This is a null, and the title of the follow-up paper identifies it as a model of the recessive disease DFNB113. The dominant disease this entry describes is caused by missense alleles whose protein is still made and still enters the matrix. The null therefore tests what happens when CEACAM16 is absent, not what happens when an abnormal monomer is present, and the dominant-negative step is the one part of this pathograph the model cannot address.

edges.description: Reproduces the functional signature directly: enlarged stimulus-frequency and transiently evoked emissions, and spontaneous emissions in most homozygotes.
edges.limitations: Young null mice retain near-normal thresholds, so the model captures early micromechanical instability rather than the established hearing loss patients present with. Mouse and human cochlear tonotopy also differ, so the frequency at which instability appears does not transfer directly.

edges.description: The model carries a null allele, so it does not produce an abnormal monomer at all and cannot test the initiating lesion of the dominant disease.
edges.limitations: No knock-in mouse carrying a human dominant CEACAM16 missense allele has been reported. The dominant-negative mechanism this entry's first two nodes assert therefore has no animal support, only the in vitro secretion assays and the human genetics.

nodes.description: The mutant monomer is handled differently by the secretory pathway. The direction differs by allele: p.Gly169Arg is secreted much less efficiently than wild type, while p.Arg255Gly is present at increased levels. Both segregate with dominant disease, which is the observation a dominant-negative model has to accommodate. See `discussions`.

evidence.reference_title: Exome sequencing identifies a novel CEACAM16 mutation associated with autosomal dominant nonsyndromic hearing loss DFNA4B in a Chinese family.
evidence.snippet: our studies in transfected HEK293T cells show that the secretion efficacy of the mutant CEACAM16 is much lower than that of the wild type, suggesting a deleterious effect of the sequence variant

nodes.description: A heterozygous missense change in a conserved immunoglobulin-like domain yields a structurally abnormal CEACAM16 monomer. The protein is still made; what changes is its folding and its handling by the secretory pathway. The reported alleles cluster in the conserved Ig domains, including the most strongly conserved N2 domain.

nodes.description: A null mouse generated to test what CEACAM16 does structurally. It reproduces the tectorial membrane matrix failure and a striking micromechanical instability, and with age shows accelerated membrane degradation and detachment.

The tectorial membrane is the passive mechanical element that loads the outer hair cell feedback loop. Disrupting it does not simply weaken amplification: it destabilises it. Young null mice have near-normal thresholds and distortion-product emissions but enlarged stimulus-frequency and transiently evoked emissions, and spontaneous emissions in about 70% of homozygotes against under 3% of wild type. That signature is a cochlear amplifier still working but no longer damped, which is a different failure from hair-cell loss.

evidence.reference_title: Loss of the tectorial membrane protein CEACAM16 enhances spontaneous, stimulus-frequency, and transiently evoked otoacoustic emissions.
evidence.snippet: We also observed spontaneous otoacoustic emissions (SOAEs) in 70% of the homozygous mice. This incidence is remarkable considering that <3% of WT controls have SOAEs.

evidence.reference_title: Loss of the tectorial membrane protein CEACAM16 enhances spontaneous, stimulus-frequency, and transiently evoked otoacoustic emissions.
evidence.snippet: Changes in TM structure appear to influence the balance between energy generation and dissipation such that the system becomes unstable.

nodes.description: CEACAM16 binds both alpha-tectorin and beta-tectorin and is proposed to cross-link them into the striated-sheet matrix. When it is absent, beta-tectorin levels fall, no defined striated-sheet matrix develops, and Hensen's stripe does not form. The dominant disease is thought to reach the same endpoint by a different route, with an abnormal monomer entering and poisoning the matrix rather than being missing from it; that step is an inference, since the structural data come from a null.

evidence.reference_title: Loss of the tectorial membrane protein CEACAM16 enhances spontaneous, stimulus-frequency, and transiently evoked otoacoustic emissions.
evidence.snippet: In the absence of CEACAM16, TECTB levels are reduced, a clearly defined striated-sheet matrix does not develop, and Hensen's stripe, a prominent feature in the basal two-thirds of the TM in WT mice, is absent.

evidence.reference_title: Loss of the tectorial membrane protein CEACAM16 enhances spontaneous, stimulus-frequency, and transiently evoked otoacoustic emissions.
evidence.snippet: CEACAM16 is also shown to interact with TECTB, indicating that it may stabilize interactions between TECTA and TECTB.

nodes.description: The loss begins at high frequencies, in the basal cochlea, and extends to middle and lower frequencies with age.

evidence.reference_title: Auditory Phenotype of a Novel Missense Variant in the CEACAM16 Gene in a Large Russian Family With Autosomal Dominant Nonsyndromic Hearing Loss.
evidence.snippet: Eleven family members suffer from hearing impairment, which starts with tinnitus and threshold increase at high frequencies, since the age of 5-20 years.

nodes.description: CEACAM16 concentrates at the point where the tectorial membrane attaches to the tips of the tallest outer hair cell stereocilia. A disordered matrix degrades that mechanical linkage, and with age the membrane itself degrades and detaches faster than normal.
nodes.id: Impaired Tectorial Membrane to Stereocilia Coupling

evidence.reference_title: Carcinoembryonic antigen-related cell adhesion molecule 16 interacts with alpha-tectorin and is mutated in autosomal dominant hearing loss (DFNA4).
evidence.snippet: its protein product localizes to the tips of the tallest stereocilia and the tectorial membrane (TM). This specific localization suggests a role in maintaining the integrity of the TM as well as in the connection between the OHC stereocilia and TM, a linkage essential for mechanical amplification.

evidence.reference_title: Accelerated Age-Related Degradation of the Tectorial Membrane in the Ceacam16(βgal/βgal) Null Mutant Mouse, a Model for Late-Onset Human Hereditary Deafness DFNB113.
evidence.snippet: The loss of Ceacam16 therefore accelerates age-related degeneration of the tectorial membrane leading, as in humans with mutations in CEACAM16, to a late-onset progressive form of hearing loss.

nodes.description: Slowly progressive over decades rather than static or stepwise, with a trajectory the reporting authors describe as similar to age-related hearing loss.

evidence.reference_title: Auditory Phenotype of a Novel Missense Variant in the CEACAM16 Gene in a Large Russian Family With Autosomal Dominant Nonsyndromic Hearing Loss.
evidence.snippet: Hearing loss slowly progresses with age in each person and is similar to age-related hearing loss.
